# Preface {.unnumbered}

Cells process information with networks of interacting proteins, genes, and
small molecules. To understand how these networks behave, we write down what
we know about their parts and interactions and ask what that knowledge
implies. Mathematical models make that question precise. This book teaches
**rule-based modeling**, an approach to building such models that suits
networks of proteins with many interaction sites, using the
[BioNetGen](https://bionetgen.org) language and tools
[@Blinov2004; @Faeder2009; @Harris2016].

## Who this book is for

The book has three audiences in mind:

- **Students** in courses on computational and systems biology. The early
  chapters assume a little calculus and some Python, but no prior modeling
  experience.
- **New members of a modeling lab** who need to become productive with
  rule-based models: building them, simulating them, fitting them to data, and
  sharing them.
- **Experimental and computational biologists** who want a practical
  introduction to the BioNetGen tools.

## How the book is organized

Each chapter introduces one set of ideas and applies them to a running
example, a cytokine signaling circuit in which STAT transcription factors
induce their own inhibitor, SOCS. The chapters are grouped into parts.

**Part I. Foundations**

- @sec-reaction-networks: Builds the
  STAT–SOCS circuit one reaction at a time and shows how a reaction network
  becomes a set of differential equations.
- @sec-rules: Shows why naming every complex
  by hand breaks down, and how rules that act on structured molecules solve
  the problem.
- @sec-stochastic: Describes reactions
  among small numbers of molecules with the chemical master equation and
  Gillespie's algorithm, and follows the noise from a single SOCS gene
  through the feedback loop.
- @sec-rules-guide: Writes rules for binding,
  enzymatic modification, synthesis and degradation, and aggregation, and
  checks each one against the reactions BioNetGen generates.

**Part II. Building realistic models**

- @sec-compartments: Places the circuit in a
  cell with a nucleus and endosomes, and shows how compartment sizes scale the
  rates of reactions.
- @sec-network-free: Simulates models whose
  networks are too large to generate, using receptor aggregation as the
  example.
- @sec-analysis: Computes conservation laws, steady
  states and their stability, dose–response curves, sensitivities, and
  bistability.
- @sec-energy-modeling: Assigns free energies to molecular structures so
  that cooperative binding satisfies detailed balance, and distinguishes
  equilibrium from signaling driven by ATP hydrolysis.

**In preparation.** Part III, *Models meet data*, will cover parameter
estimation, uncertainty and identifiability, building and sharing models, and AI-assisted modeling. Part IV
will cover advanced topics, including spatial simulation, rare events, and
visualization, and Part V will present case studies. The plan for the full
book is in
[`BOOK_PLAN.md`](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen-book/blob/main/BOOK_PLAN.md).

Every model in the book is in the
[`models/`](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen-book/tree/main/models)
folder of the book's repository, organized by chapter, and every figure is
produced by running those models. Each chapter ends with exercises. Lecture
slides and printable worksheets are available for Chapters 1 and 2 and are in
preparation for the others.

## Tools

You can run the models in this book in three ways:

1. In a web browser, with no installation, using
   [BNG Playground](https://ruleworld.github.io/bngplayground/).
2. In Visual Studio Code with the BioNetGen extension, which provides
   syntax highlighting, one-click simulation, and plotting.
3. From Python, using [bngsim](https://bngsim.readthedocs.io) for fast ODE
   and stochastic simulation. This is how the figures in the book are made,
   it runs every model in the book, and it is the route to the analysis and
   fitting covered in later chapters.

@sec-installation explains how to install them, and @sec-bngl-reference
summarizes the syntax of BNGL.

## Conventions

BNGL code is shown in shaded blocks:

```bngl
begin reaction rules
  LRbind: L(r) + R(l) <-> L(r!1).R(l!1) kon, koff
end reaction rules
```

Python code that produces a figure is shown above the figure in the web
version of the book. Unless stated otherwise, concentrations are in
micromolar (µM) and time is in minutes. The parameter values in the running
example are illustrative, chosen to show the behavior clearly rather than
fitted to a particular cell type.
